lessons.title: Classes initialize and instance state
lessons.summary: Replace second = Counter.new(8) with second = first. What prints?
explanation: class defines a class; Counter.new(2) allocates an instance and calls its initialize method with 2. initialize sets up that instance rather than returning the new object itself.

@value is an instance variable belonging to the current receiver. value += 1 means add one and store the result; here @value += 1 updates that receiver. A method returns its last expression, so advance returns the updated number.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Counter
  def initialize(start)
    @value = start
  end
  def advance
    @value += 1
  end
end
first = Counter.new(2)
second = Counter.new(8)
puts first.advance
puts second.advance
```

Expected output or behavior: 3
9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Attribute readers and controlled writes
lessons.summary: Replace goal.add_step with goal.steps = 9. What happens?
explanation: attr_reader :steps creates a public steps method that reads @steps. It does not create a steps= writer. attr_accessor would create both methods.

lessons.title: Method visibility and public boundaries
lessons.summary: Replace puts badge.label with puts badge.decorate. What happens?
explanation: Methods are normally public. private changes the default visibility of subsequent instance method definitions. decorate is an internal helper; label can call it without an explicit receiver.

An outside caller cannot use badge.decorate as a public method call. Visibility organizes an API, not a security sandbox: reflective operations can bypass some visibility restrictions. Ruby also has protected methods for restricted receiver calls within the class family; they are not public either.

```ruby
class Badge
  def label
    decorate
  end
  private
  def decorate
    "[ready]"
  end
end
badge = Badge.new
puts badge.label
```

lessons.title: Inheritance super and overriding
lessons.summary: Change super(name) to super(). What happens?
explanation: class Detail < Base establishes inheritance. Detail defines its own label method, so that implementation is selected for a Detail receiver.
super(name) calls the next implementation with that argument. Bare super forwards the current arguments; super() forwards none. This distinction matters when the parent requires an argument.

```ruby

  def label(name)
    "base:#{name}"
  end
end
class Detail < Base
  def label(name)
    super(name) + "!"
  end
end
puts Detail.new.label("map")
```

lessons.title: Prepend and method lookup
lessons.summary: Replace prepend Frame with include Frame. What prints?
explanation: prepend Frame places the module before Page in method lookup. Frame#label is found first, and super continues to Page#label.

lessons.title: Constants and namespace lookup
lessons.summary: Move Notes to a separate module Atlas::Notes body, leaving TITLE unqualified inside title. What happens?
explanation: Atlas::Notes means the Notes constant inside Atlas. Constants begin with uppercase letters. A constant can refer to a mutable object; the name alone does not freeze that object.

lessons.title: Identity equality and hash keys
lessons.summary: Change lookup.fetch(1.0, "missing") to lookup.fetch(1, "missing"). What changes?
explanation: == asks the class’s value-comparison rule; Array compares elements. equal? tests whether two references identify the very same object. Separate arrays can be value-equal without being identical.

Hash uses hash and eql? together to identify keys. Integer 1 and Float 1.0 compare equal with == but not with eql?, so they are distinct hash keys. A custom key type that overrides eql? must provide a consistent hash result for equal keys; do not mutate key identity fields while stored.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
a = [1]
b = [1]
puts a == b
puts a.equal?(b)
puts 1 == 1.0
puts 1.eql?(1.0)
lookup = {1 => "integer"}
puts lookup.fetch(1.0, "missing")
```

explanation: case/in patterns inspect structure. This hash pattern requires kind: :note and an Integer count. Integer => n both checks that value and binds it to n. Extra hash keys are allowed by this pattern.

lessons.title: Introspection and safe public dispatch
lessons.summary: Replace public_send(:title) with public_send(:secret). What follows true?
explanation: respond_to?(:title) checks whether an object advertises that operation, normally excluding private methods. It is not proof of correct arguments, results, safety or authorization.

public_send invokes only a public method; send can bypass visibility, so it is not interchangeable. When a method name comes from outside the program, validate it against a fixed allowlist as well: even public methods may be inappropriate for the requested action. Here the symbol is a fixed trusted literal.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Actions
  def title
    "ready"
  end
  private
  def secret
    "internal"
  end
end
actions = Actions.new
puts actions.respond_to?(:title)
puts actions.public_send(:title)
```

lessons.title: Define methods from explicit code
lessons.summary: Replace define_method(:scale) do |value| with def scale(value), leaving its body and end in place. What happens?
explanation: define_method(:scale) installs an instance method using the supplied block. Its parameter value becomes the method argument, and the block can capture surrounding local bindings such as factor.

A normal def body does not capture the surrounding local variables in this way. define_method is useful for a small explicit family of behaviors; it does not require eval or executing strings from users. Repeated definitions of the same method name replace earlier definitions rather than creating argument-count overloads.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Calculator
  factor = 3
  define_method(:scale) do |value|
    value * factor
  end
end
puts Calculator.new.scale(4)
```

lessons.title: Lexical refinements and lookup boundaries
lessons.summary: Move using Highlight above def earlier, leaving the rest unchanged. What prints?
explanation: refine Label defines a scoped variation of Label methods inside a module. using Highlight activates it for subsequent code in the current lexical scope; here that scope is the remainder of this source file. using cannot be called inside a method body.

A method defined before activation does not inherit the caller’s refinements just because it is called afterward. earlier was defined without Highlight active. Refinements avoid a global class rewrite, but their lexical lookup must still be understood when code crosses files or method definitions.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Label
  def text
    "plain"
  end
end
module Highlight
  refine Label do
    def text
      "bright"
    end
  end
end
def earlier(item)
  item.text
end
using Highlight
puts Label.new.text
puts earlier(Label.new)
```
